institutions.name: Studium of Palencia
institutions.summary: The first studium generale of the Iberian peninsula, created by Alfonso VIII of Castile with Bishop Tello Téllez de Meneses, bringing masters from France and Italy to teach theology, arts and law. It declined rapidly after the king's death and was overtaken by Salamanca.
institutions.notes: Foundation is variously dated 1208–1212; teaching had stopped by the mid-13th century and Urban IV's 1263 bull failed to revive it.

institutions.name: University of Salamanca
institutions.summary: Founded by Alfonso IX of León, Salamanca became the leading university of Castile and of the Spanish empire. In the 16th century it was home to the 'School of Salamanca' (Vitoria, Soto, Cano), which shaped natural law, international law and economic thought.
institutions.notes: 1218 is the conventional date of Alfonso IX's foundation; the founding charter itself does not survive.

institutions.name: University of Valladolid
institutions.summary: A studium that grew up in Valladolid in the 13th century, endowed by Sancho IV and recognised as a studium generale by Clement VI in 1346. With Salamanca and Alcalá it was one of the three 'major universities' of Castile, strong in law because of the royal Chancillería in the city.
institutions.notes: Origins are obscure: dates from c.1241 to the 1280s are given; 1346 is the papal recognition.

institutions.name: University of Coimbra
institutions.summary: Portugal's only university until the 16th century, founded by King Dinis in Lisbon and moved between Lisbon and Coimbra until it settled in Coimbra in 1537. The Pombaline reform of 1772 turned it into one of the most modern scientific universities of Enlightenment Europe.
institutions.notes: Dinis's 'Scientiae thesaurus mirabilis' is dated 1 March 1290; Nicholas IV's bull followed on 9 August 1290.

institutions.name: University of Lleida
institutions.summary: The first university of the Crown of Aragon, founded by James II with the city council, which granted it a monopoly on higher studies in his realms. Strong in law, it trained Aragonese jurists and clergy until Philip V closed it under the Nueva Planta decrees.
institutions.notes: Boniface VIII's bull authorising a studium was issued in 1297; James II's founding privilege dates from 1 September 1300.

institutions.name: University of Perpignan
institutions.summary: Founded by Peter IV of Aragon for Roussillon, then part of the Crown of Aragon, and confirmed by the Avignon pope Clement VII. It passed to France with Roussillon in 1659 and lasted until the French Revolution.

institutions.name: University of Huesca
institutions.summary: Founded by Peter IV of Aragon and refounded by John II with papal approval in 1464, Huesca (called 'Sertoriana' after Sertorius's legendary school) was the main university of Upper Aragon. It was suppressed by the Plan Pidal in 1845.
institutions.notes: Teaching appears to have lapsed in the 14th–15th centuries before the 1464 refoundation.

institutions.name: University of Alcalá / Central University of Madrid
institutions.summary: Founded by Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros around the Colegio Mayor de San Ildefonso as a Renaissance university devoted to theology and the three biblical languages; it produced the Complutensian Polyglot Bible (1514–17). Moved to Madrid in 1836, it became the Universidad Central, the only Spanish university allowed to grant doctorates after 1845.
institutions.notes: Bull of Alexander VI 13 April 1499; teaching began in 1508. A 1293 studium of Sancho IV at Alcalá was a precursor without continuity.

institutions.name: University of Sigüenza
alt: Colegio de San Antonio de Portaceli
institutions.summary: Grew from the Colegio de San Antonio de Portaceli, founded in 1476 by the canon Juan López de Medina, and was raised to a university by Innocent VIII. A small 'minor university' that survived until the Bourbon reforms reduced it.
institutions.notes: Suppressed 1807 but the order was not carried out; academic activity ended in 1824.

institutions.name: University of Seville
alt: Colegio de Santa María de Jesús
institutions.summary: Founded on the Colegio de Santa María de Jesús of archdeacon Rodrigo Fernández de Santaella ('Maese Rodrigo'), and the main university of Andalusia, linked to the American trade of Seville. Pablo de Olavide's 1769 plan made it a showcase of Enlightenment reform.
institutions.notes: A 1502 royal cédula had authorised the city to found a studium; Julius II's bull for Santaella's college dates from 1505.

institutions.name: University of Santiago de Compostela
institutions.summary: Began as a grammar school for poor clerics founded by Lope Gómez de Marzoa and developed by Diego de Muros and Archbishop Alonso III de Fonseca, whose college gave it university status. The university of Galicia.
institutions.notes: 1495 is the conventional date; university status was confirmed by papal bulls of the 1520s–1550s.

institutions.name: University of Zaragoza
institutions.summary: Granted university privileges by Charles I in 1542 on the basis of an older arts school, it effectively opened in 1583 under Bishop Pedro Cerbuna. Aragon's main university, its buildings suffered heavily in the Napoleonic sieges.
institutions.notes: A 1474 bull of Sixtus IV for a general study of arts is the earliest root; 1542 is the university's official foundation and 1583 the real opening.

institutions.name: University of Granada
institutions.summary: Founded by Charles V after his 1526 stay in Granada to Christianise and educate the former Nasrid kingdom, and confirmed by Clement VII in 1531. It later became the district university of eastern Andalusia.
institutions.notes: Royal decision 1526; papal bull 1531.

institutions.name: University of Toledo
institutions.summary: Based on the Colegio de Santa Catalina founded in 1485 by the canon Francisco Álvarez de Toledo, which a bull of Leo X raised to university status. A minor university closed in the 19th-century rationalisation.

institutions.name: University of Oviedo
institutions.summary: Founded under the will of the Inquisitor General Fernando de Valdés Salas, with papal approval in 1574, and opened in 1608. The university of Asturias, it had Feijoo as its most famous Enlightenment professor.
institutions.notes: Valdés's bequest 1566–68; bull of Gregory XIII 1574; formal opening 21 September 1608.

institutions.name: University of Osuna
institutions.summary: Founded by Juan Téllez-Girón, fourth Count of Ureña, with a bull of Paul III, as a college-university for his seigneurial town. A typical minor Castilian university, suppressed in the 19th-century reforms.

institutions.name: University of Oñati
institutions.summary: The only university of the Basque Country before modern times, founded by Bishop Rodrigo Mercado de Zuazola with a bull of Paul III, in a notable Plateresque building. It survived repeated closures until 1901.
institutions.notes: Closed definitively in 1901 (after this dataset's scope), hence end=null. Repeatedly suppressed and reopened (1807, 1842, Carlist reopening in the 1870s, Catholic free university 1895–1901); some details are uncertain. Some sources mention a first seat at Hernani.

institutions.name: University of Baeza
institutions.summary: Founded by a bull of Paul III on a grammar school endowed by Rodrigo López, and organised by St John of Ávila. Known for training clergy in the 'Ávila school' spirituality.

institutions.name: University of Gandia
institutions.summary: Founded at the request of Francis Borgia, Duke of Gandia, and entrusted to the Jesuits: the first university of the Society of Jesus. Its constitutions served as a model for later Jesuit universities.

institutions.name: University of Évora
institutions.summary: Portugal's second university, founded by Cardinal Henry, Archbishop of Évora, and run by the Jesuits. It was a major centre of Jesuit scholastic theology until Pombal expelled the Society.

institutions.name: University of Cervera
alt: Real y Pontificia Universidad de Cervera
institutions.summary: Created by Philip V after the Nueva Planta decrees to replace all the Catalan universities, as a reward to Cervera for its loyalty in the War of the Spanish Succession. It was Catalonia's only university until its transfer to Barcelona in 1842.
institutions.notes: Briefly moved to Barcelona during the Liberal Triennium (1822–23).

institutions.name: University of Mallorca
institutions.summary: Grew out of the Lullist school of Palma, made a general study by Ferdinand II in 1483 and a full Universitat Literària in 1692. It disappeared during the 19th-century liberal reforms.
institutions.notes: Papal confirmation 1673 (Clement X) and royal ratification 1692. Final closure is variously given as 1829/30 or 1842–46; replaced by the Institut Balear.

institutions.name: University of Santo Tomás of Ávila
institutions.summary: A Dominican convent-university in the royal monastery of Santo Tomás. A small institution mainly for theology and arts.
institutions.notes: Founding date and final closure are approximate; reduced to a college under the 1824 Calomarde plan.

institutions.name: University of Almagro
alt: Universidad de Nuestra Señora del Rosario
institutions.summary: A Dominican college-university in the Calatrava town of Almagro, founded on the bequest of Fernando Fernández de Córdoba and opened in 1574. Suppressed in the Bourbon rationalisation.

institutions.name: University of Orihuela
institutions.summary: A Dominican college founded in 1547 by Archbishop Fernando de Loazes and raised to a university by Pius V. It served the southern Kingdom of Valencia.

institutions.name: University of Tarragona
institutions.summary: Founded by Archbishop Gaspar Cervantes de Gaeta as a post-Tridentine university, confirmed by Gregory XIII and opened in 1577. Closed under the Nueva Planta.

institutions.name: University of Vic
institutions.summary: A municipal university granted degree rights in arts and philosophy by Philip III. One of seven Catalan universities closed by Philip V.

institutions.name: University of Girona
institutions.summary: Alfonso V granted Girona a general study in 1446, but regular teaching only began in 1572 in the Les Àligues building. Closed under the Nueva Planta.

institutions.name: University of Solsona
institutions.summary: The Dominican college of Sant Miquel i Sant Gabriel (1615), made a literary university by a bull of Paul V. Merged into Cervera in 1717.

institutions.name: University of Tortosa
institutions.summary: A Dominican university linked to the Royal Colleges of Tortosa, which granted degrees in arts and theology. Closed under the Nueva Planta.
institutions.notes: Dominican higher studies date back to 1529; university status around 1600 is approximate.

institutions.name: University of Sahagún
institutions.summary: The Benedictine monastery of San Facundo at Sahagún was given degree-granting powers by Clement VII. The Benedictines' university was later transferred to Irache.
institutions.notes: The transfer date (Paul V's approval 1605) is approximate.

institutions.name: University of Irache
alt: Universidad de Santa María la Real de Irache
institutions.summary: The Benedictine university of the Congregation of Valladolid in Navarre, at the monastery of Irache near Estella. It granted many degrees, especially in theology and arts.
institutions.notes: A college of arts and theology existed from c.1544; university status c.1569; papal confirmation 1616. Closure is variously 1807 or 1824.

institutions.name: University of Santa Catalina (El Burgo de Osma)
institutions.summary: Founded by Bishop Pedro Álvarez de Acosta and authorised by Julius III. A minor Castilian university where Jovellanos studied.
institutions.notes: Closed 1807–1814 and 1833–1839; final closure 1841–42; some sources say it was moved to Soria in 1839.

institutions.name: Dominican University of Pamplona
institutions.summary: A Dominican convent university in Pamplona, granting degrees in arts and theology. Suppressed under Charles III.

institutions.name: University of Murcia (19th century)
institutions.summary: A short-lived university proclaimed by Murcia's revolutionary junta in 1840 and suppressed the following year, then revived as a free university in 1869–74. The present university dates from 1915.
institutions.notes: Ended 1874 for lack of money and students.

institutions.name: University of San Fernando (La Laguna)
institutions.summary: The first university of the Canary Islands, decreed by Ferdinand VII and opened in the former Jesuit college of La Laguna. It was abolished by the Plan Pidal; the present university was restored in 1927.
institutions.notes: A 1792 decree of Charles IV and an Augustinian university (bull 1744) never took effect. Ferdinand VII's decree is from 1816.

institutions.name: University of Valencia
institutions.summary: Founded by the city council of Valencia and confirmed by Alexander VI and Ferdinand II, it was a centre of Renaissance humanism and medicine. Its 1786 Plan Blasco was an important Enlightenment reform.

institutions.name: University of Barcelona
institutions.summary: Created by the Consell de Cent on a privilege of Alfonso V, it was consolidated in the 16th century. Suppressed by Philip V in 1717, it was restored in 1837–42 by moving the University of Cervera to Barcelona.
institutions.notes: Teaching of medicine existed from 1401. The 1717–1837 suppression is treated as an interruption, as the restored university claims continuity.

institutions.name: Royal Patriotic Seminary of Vergara
institutions.summary: Founded by the Royal Basque Society of Friends of the Country as an Enlightenment school with chairs of chemistry and mineralogy. In its laboratory the Elhuyar brothers isolated tungsten in 1783.
institutions.notes: Became a royal Seminario de Nobles c.1804 and later a secondary school; the end of its higher-level scientific role is approximate.

institutions.name: Mining Academy of Almadén / School of Mining Engineers of Madrid
institutions.summary: Spain's first mining school, created by Charles III at the mercury mines of Almadén on the model of Freiberg. In 1835 it was moved to Madrid as the Escuela de Minas, with Almadén keeping a practical school.

institutions.name: School of Civil Engineering of Madrid
alt: Escuela de Caminos, Canales y Puertos
institutions.summary: Founded by Agustín de Betancourt on the model of the École des Ponts et Chaussées to train the state corps of road and canal engineers. It closed during war and absolutist reaction and was restored in 1834.

institutions.name: Royal College of Artillery of Segovia
institutions.summary: The artillery academy founded by Charles III in the Alcázar of Segovia under Félix Gazola, with strong teaching in mathematics and chemistry. Louis Proust ran its chemistry laboratory, where he worked on the law of definite proportions.
institutions.notes: During the Napoleonic war the college moved temporarily to the south.

institutions.name: Royal Academy of Naval Guards
institutions.summary: The naval academy founded by José Patiño in Cádiz, which taught mathematics, astronomy and navigation and had an important observatory. It trained Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa.
institutions.notes: Closing date approximate; a naval college reopened at San Fernando in 1845.

institutions.name: Royal Military Academy of Mathematics of Barcelona
institutions.summary: The training school of the Spanish corps of military engineers, founded by Philip V's engineer-general Jorge Próspero de Verboom and directed by Mateo Calabro and Pedro de Lucuce.
institutions.notes: Founding year 1720 (opened c.1720); end approximate.

institutions.name: Royal Veterinary School of Madrid
institutions.summary: Spain's first veterinary school, founded on the model of Alfort. It trained army and civilian veterinarians.
institutions.notes: Founded 1792; teaching started 1793.

institutions.name: School of Forestry Engineers
alt: Escuela Especial de Ingenieros de Montes
institutions.summary: Spain's school of forestry engineering on the German (Tharandt) model, founded by Agustín Pascual and Esteban Boutelou.
institutions.notes: Decreed 1846; opened 1848.

institutions.name: Royal Industrial Institute of Madrid
institutions.summary: Spain's first school of industrial engineering, a central institute created during the reorganisation of technical education. It was closed for lack of funds.

institutions.name: Industrial School of Barcelona
alt: Escuela de Ingenieros Industriales de Barcelona
institutions.summary: The industrial engineering school of Catalonia, the centre of Spanish industry, created from the Junta de Comercio's earlier chairs.

institutions.name: School of Agricultural Engineers
institutions.summary: The central school of agronomy, opened at the La Flamenca estate near Aranjuez and later moved to Madrid.
institutions.notes: Relocation date approximate.

institutions.name: School of Architecture of Madrid
institutions.summary: Created by separating architectural teaching from the Royal Academy of San Fernando, it became the professional school of Spanish architects.

institutions.name: Polytechnic School of Lisbon
institutions.summary: Created by Sá da Bandeira in the former Royal College of Nobles (1761) to teach mathematics and science as preparation for army and engineering careers. It was Portugal's main science school outside Coimbra.

institutions.name: Polytechnic Academy of Porto
alt: Academia Real da Marinha e Comércio
institutions.summary: Founded as the Royal Academy of Navy and Commerce, it became the Polytechnic Academy in 1837, training engineers and pilots for Porto's trade and industry.

institutions.name: Medical-Surgical School of Lisbon
alt: Real Escola de Cirurgia de Lisboa
institutions.summary: Founded as the Royal School of Surgery at the hospital of São José, it became a medical-surgical school in 1836. It was a rival to Coimbra's faculty of medicine.

institutions.name: Medical-Surgical School of Porto
alt: Real Escola de Cirurgia do Porto
institutions.summary: Founded as the Royal School of Surgery of Porto, it became a medical-surgical school in 1836.

institutions.name: Higher Course of Letters (Lisbon)
institutions.summary: A higher school of humanities endowed by King Pedro V, Portugal's first state institution for literature, history and philosophy outside Coimbra.

institutions.name: Royal College of Surgery of Cádiz
alt: Real Colegio de Cirugía de la Armada
institutions.summary: Founded by Pedro Virgili to train surgeons for the Spanish navy, it introduced modern anatomy and surgery to Spain. It became a faculty of medicine in 1843.

institutions.name: Royal College of Surgery of Barcelona
alt: Real Colegio de Cirugía de Barcelona
institutions.summary: The second royal college of surgery, founded by Pedro Virgili; in the absence of a university in Barcelona it was the city's main medical school. Merged into the University of Barcelona in 1843.

institutions.name: Royal College of Surgery of San Carlos
alt: Real Colegio de Cirugía de San Carlos
institutions.summary: The royal surgical college of Madrid, founded by Antonio Gimbernat and Mariano Ribas. It became the faculty of medicine of the University of Madrid in 1843.

institutions.name: Colegio Imperial / Reales Estudios de San Isidro
institutions.summary: The Jesuit college of Madrid, founded on Empress Maria's bequest and raised by Philip IV into the Reales Estudios with chairs in mathematics, sciences and languages. After the 1767 expulsion it continued as the state-run Reales Estudios de San Isidro.
institutions.notes: Became a secondary Instituto in 1845; end approximate.

institutions.name: Jesuit College of Santo Antão
institutions.summary: The main Jesuit college of Lisbon, whose 'Aula da Esfera' (from c.1590) was the leading school of mathematics, astronomy and navigation in Portugal. Closed by Pombal's expulsion of the Jesuits.

events.title: Alfonso VIII founds the studium
events.desc: Alfonso VIII of Castile, with Bishop Tello, establishes salaried masters in theology, arts and law at Palencia (date conventional, 1208–1212).

events.title: Urban IV grants Paris privileges
events.desc: Pope Urban IV grants the studium the privileges of Paris in an attempt to revive it; the attempt failed and the school disappears.

events.title: Alfonso IX founds the studium
events.desc: Alfonso IX of León establishes 'scolas' at Salamanca, the conventional foundation of the university.

events.title: Charter of Alfonso X
events.desc: Alfonso X 'the Wise' issues a royal charter endowing chairs in law, canon law, medicine, logic, grammar and music, and regulating the studium.

events.title: Papal recognition by Alexander IV
events.desc: Pope Alexander IV confirms Salamanca as a studium generale and grants its graduates the licentia ubique docendi (except Paris and Bologna).

events.title: Constitutions of Benedict XIII
events.desc: The Avignon pope Benedict XIII (Pedro de Luna) issues constitutions and founds a faculty of theology, also funding the Escuelas Mayores.

events.title: Constitutions of Martin V
events.desc: Martin V's constitutions fix the university's governance (rector, consiliarios, claustro), its basic statutes until the 18th century.

events.title: Plan de estudios of Charles III
events.desc: Charles III's government imposes a new plan of studies, modernising curricula after the expulsion of the Jesuits.

events.title: Caballero plan
events.desc: The Caballero reform imposes Salamanca's plan of studies on all Spanish universities and suppresses eleven minor universities.

events.title: Napoleonic demolitions
events.desc: During the French occupation and the 1812 Arapiles campaign, many colleges and university buildings were demolished for fortifications.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: The Plan Pidal centralises Spanish universities under the state, reducing them to ten district universities with uniform curricula; Salamanca loses doctoral rights to Madrid.

events.title: Abolition of the theology faculty
events.desc: After the 1868 revolution, the state abolishes faculties of theology, ending Salamanca's most historic faculty.

events.title: Emergence of the studium
events.desc: A studium is attested at Valladolid in the 13th century, likely transferred from or influenced by Palencia; date conventional.

events.title: Endowment by Sancho IV
events.desc: Sancho IV grants royal revenues (tercias) to support the studium.

events.title: Bull of Clement VI
events.desc: Pope Clement VI recognises Valladolid as a studium generale with the privileges of Paris and Bologna (without theology).

events.title: Faculty of theology
events.desc: Pope Martin V authorises a faculty of theology.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Retained as one of the ten state district universities under the Plan Pidal.

events.title: King Dinis founds the Estudo Geral
events.desc: King Dinis issues 'Scientiae thesaurus mirabilis' (1 March 1290) founding a general study in Lisbon.

events.title: Bull of Nicholas IV
events.desc: Pope Nicholas IV confirms the Lisbon studium generale with faculties of arts, canon law, civil law and medicine.

events.title: Move to Coimbra
events.desc: Dinis transfers the university to Coimbra after conflicts between students and Lisbon townsmen.

events.title: Return to Lisbon
events.desc: Afonso IV moves the university back to Lisbon.

events.title: Back to Coimbra
events.desc: Afonso IV returns the university to Coimbra.

events.title: Back to Lisbon
events.desc: King Fernando moves the university to Lisbon, where it stays for 160 years.

events.title: Definitive move to Coimbra
events.desc: John III transfers the university permanently to Coimbra, later installing it in the royal palace (Paço das Escolas).

events.title: Colégio das Artes handed to the Jesuits
events.desc: John III gives the preparatory Colégio das Artes, founded 1548 with humanists from Bordeaux, to the Society of Jesus.

events.title: Expulsion of the Jesuits
events.desc: Pombal expels the Jesuits from Portugal, removing them from the Colégio das Artes and university teaching.

events.title: Pombaline reform
events.desc: New statutes create faculties of mathematics and philosophy (natural sciences), with a botanical garden, observatory, chemistry laboratory and natural history museum.

events.title: Liberal reform
events.desc: After the dissolution of the religious orders (1834), Passos Manuel's reform merges canon and civil law faculties (into the faculty of law) and reorganises the university.

events.title: First woman student
events.desc: Domitila de Carvalho enrols in mathematics, the first woman admitted to the University of Coimbra.

events.title: Privilege of James II
events.desc: James II of Aragon issues the founding privilege, following Boniface VIII's 1297 bull, and grants the studium a monopoly in the Crown of Aragon.

events.title: Bourbon siege of Lleida
events.desc: Philip V's troops storm Lleida in the War of the Spanish Succession; teaching is disrupted and the cathedral turned into a fortress.

events.title: Nueva Planta suppression
events.desc: Philip V suppresses the Catalan universities and concentrates teaching at Cervera.

events.title: Privilege of Peter IV
events.desc: Peter IV 'the Ceremonious' founds a studium generale at Perpignan.

events.title: Bull of Clement VII
events.desc: The Avignon pope Clement VII confirms the university and adds theology.

events.title: Transfer to the French crown
events.desc: The Treaty of the Pyrenees cedes Roussillon to France; the university comes under French royal control.

events.title: Revolutionary suppression
events.desc: Abolished with all French universities by the revolutionary Convention.

events.title: Privilege of Peter IV
events.desc: Peter IV grants Huesca a studium generale with the privileges of Lleida, Toulouse and Montpellier.

events.title: Refoundation by John II
events.desc: John II of Aragon restores the studium, confirmed by a bull of Paul II.

events.title: Suppressed by Plan Pidal
events.desc: The Plan Pidal abolishes the university, leaving Aragon served by Zaragoza.

events.title: Bull of Alexander VI for Cisneros
events.desc: Alexander VI authorises Cisneros's Colegio de San Ildefonso as a university; teaching opened in 1508.

events.title: Plan de estudios
events.desc: Charles III's reform plan imposes new curricula on Alcalá, reducing the power of the colegios mayores.

events.title: Transfer to Madrid
events.desc: The liberal government moves the university from Alcalá to Madrid, where it becomes the Universidad Literaria, renamed Universidad Central in 1850.

events.title: Absorbs the Colegio de San Carlos
events.desc: The Royal College of Surgery of San Carlos is merged into the university's new faculty of medicine.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: The Universidad Central is made the only university in Spain allowed to grant doctorates.

events.title: Ley Moyano
events.desc: The Moyano Law fixes the centralised structure of Spanish education, with Madrid at its apex.

events.title: First doctorates for women
events.desc: Dolors Aleu and Martina Castells receive doctorates in medicine at Madrid, the first women doctors from a Spanish university.

events.title: Bull of Innocent VIII
events.desc: Innocent VIII raises the Colegio de San Antonio de Portaceli to university status (30 April 1489).

events.title: Caballero plan
events.desc: Listed for suppression in the 1807 reform; the Napoleonic invasion prevented its execution.

events.title: Final closure
events.desc: Calomarde's plan reduces the university to a college, ending university teaching.

events.title: Bull of Julius II
events.desc: Julius II grants the Colegio de Santa María de Jesús the right to confer degrees.

events.title: Plan of Olavide
events.desc: Pablo de Olavide's reform separates university and college, and the university moves to the former Jesuit Casa Profesa (1771).

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Seville becomes one of the ten state district universities, also covering Cádiz medicine.

events.title: Estudio of Lope Gómez de Marzoa
events.desc: Lope Gómez de Marzoa founds a study house for clerics, later the nucleus of the university.

events.title: Fonseca's college
events.desc: Archbishop Alonso de Fonseca founds the Colegio de Santiago Alfeo and obtains papal bulls granting it university privileges.

events.title: Plan de estudios
events.desc: Charles III's reform plan is applied to Santiago.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Retained as Galicia's district university under the Plan Pidal.

events.title: Privilege of Charles I
events.desc: Charles I grants Zaragoza a general study with university privileges.

events.title: Opening under Pedro Cerbuna
events.desc: Bishop Pedro Cerbuna funds and organises the university, which begins regular teaching.

events.title: Sieges of Zaragoza
events.desc: The university buildings are badly damaged in the French sieges of 1808–1809.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Becomes the district university for all Aragon after Huesca's suppression.

events.title: Bull of Clement VII
events.desc: Clement VII confirms the university founded by Charles V's 1526 decision.

events.title: Move into the former Jesuit college
events.desc: After the Jesuit expulsion the university is reorganised and occupies the former Jesuit college.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Retained as one of the ten district universities.

events.title: Bull of Leo X
events.desc: Leo X grants the Colegio de Santa Catalina university privileges.

events.title: Caballero plan
events.desc: Suppressed by the 1807 reform.

events.title: Restoration
events.desc: Reopened after the Napoleonic war.

events.title: Suppressed by Plan Pidal
events.desc: Finally abolished in the Plan Pidal reorganisation.

events.title: Opening of the university
events.desc: The university opens, decades after Valdés's bequest and the 1574 bull of Gregory XIII.

events.title: Plan Pidal
events.desc: Retained as one of the ten district universities.

events.title: Bull of Paul III
events.desc: Paul III authorises the college-university founded by the Count of Ureña.

events.title: Caballero plan
events.desc: Suppressed by the 1807 reform; teaching was disrupted by the war.

events.title: Precarious revival
events.desc: Teaching resumes after the Napoleonic war.

events.title: Definitive closure
events.desc: Closed definitively under Calomarde's plan.

events.title: Bull of Paul III
events.desc: Paul III authorises the university founded by Bishop Mercado de Zuazola; building began in 1543.

events.title: Caballero plan
events.desc: Included among the minor universities suppressed in 1807.

events.title: Closure
events.desc: Closed by the liberal government after the First Carlist War.

events.title: Carlist university
events.desc: During the Third Carlist War the Carlists reopen it as the Real y Pontificia Universidad Vasco-Navarra.

events.title: Catholic free university
events.desc: Reopened as a Catholic free university, closing for lack of funds in 1901.

events.title: Bull of Paul III
events.desc: Paul III's bull establishes the university.
